turn2.differences: My r3 as originally phrased added a sub-clause requiring the folder to be 'the only Favorites folder' modified by Leo Park in isolation. In the data, four Favorites folders (7101, 7104, 7105, 7106) are all last-modified by Leo Park, so that sub-clause is never true on its own - uniqueness only emerges once r3 is combined with r4 (created in August) and r5 (holds exactly two files). I applied r3 in grading as simply 'modified_by is Leo Park' and let the conjunction of r3+r4+r5 do the disambiguating work, which is the natural reading of the request and correctly isolates 7101 as the sole match. Aside from that wording issue, the six conditions capture the request accurately.

ambiguity_effects.phrase: created in August 2026 (timezone for the boundary)
ambiguity_effects.explain: All candidate creation timestamps sit comfortably inside or outside August 2026 (e.g. 2026-08-20T15:00Z, 2026-09-01T15:00Z, 2026-03-10T15:00Z) with no record within a few hours of the month boundary, so choosing UTC vs. Jordan Lee's local timezone would not move any record across the line or change which folder is selected.

ambiguity_effects.phrase: holds exactly two files (direct children vs. recursive/nested count)
ambiguity_effects.explain: Only one candidate (7100) has a subfolder (7102) whose files could be counted recursively, and under either reading its total (1 direct or 3 recursive) still isn't exactly two, so it fails r5 either way. No other candidate has nested files, so the winning folder (7101) and every rejection remain the same under both readings.

turn2.naturalness_note: The request is understandable and something a user managing several similarly-named 'Audit...' folders might plausibly write, but stacking three independent disambiguating filters (modifier, creation month, file count) in one sentence is denser than typical casual phrasing - it reads like a constructed test case designed to require checking multiple near-miss folders rather than a spontaneous everyday request.
